content: The 2018 HCV care and treatment guidelines emphasize several critical strategies to improve patient outcomes. These include enhancing the transition from testing to care and treatment, promoting adherence to long-term antiviral therapy, and ensuring retention in care while re-engaging those who have disengaged. Integration of hepatitis testing, care, and treatment with other health services is recommended, alongside decentralizing these services to primary health facilities or HIV/antiretroviral clinics to improve accessibility. Task-sharing among healthcare workers and peer workers, supported by training and mentoring, is also encouraged. A differentiated care strategy is advised to assess individual care needs, with specialist referrals for complex cases. Community engagement and peer support are highlighted as essential to improving access to services and maintaining continuity of care. The implementation of these guidelines must be accompanied by efforts to uphold the human rights of individuals requiring hepatitis services. This includes ensuring informed consent, preventing stigma and discrimination, and promoting gender equity. Structural barriers such as stigma, discrimination, criminalization, and violence, particularly following a hepatitis B diagnosis, must be addressed. These barriers disproportionately affect women, young girls, adolescents, and key populations across the HIV and hepatitis care continuum. The updated WHO guidelines on HIV services for key populations outline strategies to create an enabling environment, including supportive legislation and policies, financial commitments, community empowerment, and addressing violence against key populations. Workforce training to combat stigma and discrimination and support for individuals experiencing violence are also emphasized to ensure equitable access to safe and effective healthcare services. The implementation of these recommendations should be tailored to the local context, considering factors such as national HBV epidemiology, health system and laboratory capacity, drug and commodity supply systems, financial resources, and the anticipated cost-effectiveness of interventions. Hepatitis B infection is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), an enveloped DNA virus. HBV infection can be acute or chronic, ranging from asymptomatic or mild disease to severe or fulminant hepatitis. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is defined by the presence of detectable HBsAg in the blood or serum for more than six months and encompasses a spectrum of disease. The risk of chronic infection is influenced by the age of exposure, with chronicity being more common following childhood acquisition. Globally, an estimated 296 million people are chronic carriers of HBsAg, with age-specific HBsAg seroprevalence varying significantly by geographical region. Nearly half of the global population resides in areas of high endemicity. The prevalence of HBeAg-negative disease has increased over the past decade as the HBV-infected population ages, accounting for most cases in some regions. Without effective intervention, HBV-related complications, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cirrhosis, are projected to cause 14 million deaths by 2034. HBV is primarily transmitted through percutaneous or mucosal exposure to infected blood and body fluids, including saliva, menstrual and vaginal discharge, seminal fluid, colostrum, and breast milk. Transmission can occur during medical, surgical, and dental procedures, through contaminated sharp objects, inadequately sterilized syringes and needles, intravenous and percutaneous drug use, tattooing, body piercing, and acupuncture. Sexual transmission and vertical transmission (mother-to-child) are also significant routes of HBV spread, particularly in regions like China, Southeast Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa. Mothers with high HBV DNA levels or HBeAg positivity are at high risk of transmitting the infection to their infants without prophylaxis. HBV can also cluster within family groups. The natural history of CHB is dynamic and complex, ranging from asymptomatic infection to severe chronic liver disease and HCC. While some individuals with CHB do not develop significant liver disease, others experience progressive liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, and an increased risk of HCC. Longitudinal studies indicate an 8–20% cumulative risk of cirrhosis over five years among untreated individuals with CHB. Those with cirrhosis face a 20% annual risk of hepatic decompensation, and the risk of HBV-related HCC ranges from <1% to 5%. Untreated individuals with decompensated cirrhosis have a poor prognosis, with 15–40% survival at five years. Host and viral factors can accelerate disease progression and increase the risk of HCC. In endemic regions, late diagnosis often results in the first presentation being complications of cirrhosis or HCC. CHB progresses through distinct phases characterized by virological, serological, clinical, and histological features. These phases are defined by serum aminotransferase levels, HBeAg status, serum HBV DNA concentrations, and newer biomarkers. HBeAg-positive infection is marked by high HBV replication, normal or near-normal ALT levels, minimal liver inflammation, and slow fibrosis progression. This phase is common among children and young adults infected at birth or early childhood. HBeAg-positive disease may transition to a stage of active inflammatory disease with elevated ALT and reduced HBV DNA levels due to cytolytic T-cell responses targeting infected hepatocytes. Spontaneous seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe occurs in some individuals, leading to a decline in HBV DNA and ALT levels. These individuals, often referred to as inactive carriers, typically exhibit low HBV DNA levels (<2000 IU/mL) and near-normal ALT levels, although HBsAg concentrations may remain high. HBeAg-negative disease, characterized by mutations in the precore or basal core promoter regions, is associated with continued HBV replication despite the absence of HBeAg. This phase is marked by fluctuating ALT levels, lower HBV DNA concentrations (10³–10⁵ IU/mL), and a more rapid progression to cirrhosis. Differentiating between anti-HBe-positive infection and disease requires longitudinal monitoring of HBV DNA and ALT levels. Occult HBV infection, defined by the persistence of HBV DNA in the liver or serum despite undetectable HBsAg, poses a risk of reactivation, particularly in individuals receiving potent immunosuppressive therapy. Occult infection can also contribute to new infections in blood transfusion services when HBsAg is used as the sole marker of infection. Approximately 20% of individuals with hepatitis B develop major extrahepatic manifestations, such as glomerulonephritis and arthritis, which can significantly impact quality of life and mortality. Treatment with nucleoside analogues has improved the management of these manifestations, particularly in HBsAg-positive individuals undergoing kidney transplantation or dialysis. Prevention of HBV infection through vaccination is a cornerstone of public health efforts. WHO recommends that all infants receive 3–4 doses of the HBV vaccine, with the first dose administered within 24 hours of birth. Preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) from highly viraemic mothers requires both birth-dose vaccination and pre-emptive antiviral therapy for the mother. In regions with intermediate or low endemicity, catch-up vaccination and other preventive strategies are essential for older children, adolescents, and adults at risk of HBV infection. Screening for HBV infection is critical for identifying individuals at risk and linking them to care. WHO recommends focused testing for high-risk groups, including household and sexual contacts of CHB patients, people living with HIV, individuals who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, indigenous populations, incarcerated individuals, and transgender people. Routine HBsAg screening of all pregnant women is recommended as part of integrated antenatal care services. Testing strategies should leverage existing facility-based and community-based opportunities to maximize coverage and linkage to care. Diagnosis and staging of HBV infection involve routine assessment of HBsAg-positive individuals to guide management and determine the need for treatment. This includes evaluating liver function, HBV DNA levels, and other clinical parameters to inform treatment decisions and monitor disease progression.
